metadataDescription: Split starlight and read its dark lines: Kirchhoff's bench, Fraunhofer's Sun, the spectral sequence and mystery spectra, computed from NIST atomic data and real model atmospheres.

kirchhoff.title: Kirchhoff's bench
kirchhoff.hint: Shine a lamp through a gas: dark lines, bright lines, and why.

sun.title: The Sun
sun.hint: Fraunhofer's dark lines, and the atoms that make them.

stars.title: Spectral sequence
stars.hint: The same atoms at different temperatures give different spectra.

mystery.title: Mystery spectra
mystery.hint: Which elements, and how fast is the source moving?

spectrum.label: Spectrum
spectrum.keys: Left and right arrows step between lines, Shift with an arrow pans, plus and minus zoom, 0 shows the whole range.

card.bright: bright, gas hotter than the light behind

regimeNote.weak: Few atoms absorb, so the line grows in proportion to their number. Weak lines measure abundances best.
regimeNote.saturated: The core is already as dark as it gets; more atoms barely deepen it. Thermal and turbulent motion set its width.
regimeNote.damped: Only the wings still grow, as the square root of the number of atoms. Pressure broadening sets their width.
regimeNote.stark: Only the wings still grow, as about the 2/5 power of the number of atoms: hydrogen's Stark wings fall off faster than a collision-broadened line's. The electric fields of nearby ions set their width.

notes.caK: Ionized calcium's resonance line, the strongest in the Sun's visible spectrum. Calcium is rare, but nearly every calcium atom in the Sun is ionized and in its ground state, ready to absorb.
notes.caH: K's partner: the same lower level, the other fine-structure upper level, half the oscillator strength.
notes.hDelta: Balmer line from n = 2 to n = 6. Higher in the series, the lines crowd toward the Balmer limit at 364.6 nm.
notes.ca4227: Neutral calcium's resonance line. Strong in cool stars, gone in hot ones, where calcium is ionized.
notes.gBand: Fraunhofer's G: iron and calcium lines blended with molecular CH bands, which the lab does not model.
notes.hGamma: Balmer line from n = 2 to n = 5.
notes.fe4383: One of iron's strongest visible lines. Iron's thousands of lines fill the Sun's blue spectrum.
notes.he4471: Neutral helium from a level 21 eV up: only stars hotter than about 10,000 K excite it. A key line for classifying B stars.
notes.mg4481: Ionized magnesium from a level 8.9 eV up: strongest in A stars, and a temperature gauge beside He I 447.1.
notes.he4686: Ionized helium, from a level 48 eV above its ground state. It marks the O stars.
notes.hBeta: Balmer line from n = 2 to n = 4. Its wings, widened by the electric fields of nearby ions, measure a star's surface pressure.
notes.mgB: Magnesium's b triplet, from a metastable level 2.7 eV up. Its wings grow with surface gravity, telling dwarfs from giants.
notes.heD3: Seen in the Sun's chromosphere in 1868 at a wavelength no known element matched: the discovery of helium. The photosphere is too cool to absorb it.
notes.naD: Sodium's resonance doublet, the yellow of street lamps and of Bunsen's flame. Strong in cool stars and in cold interstellar gas.
notes.hAlpha: Balmer line from n = 2 to n = 3: the red of glowing hydrogen. Its strength places a star on the spectral sequence.
notes.li6708: Lithium's resonance line, the crimson of a lithium flame. Stars destroy lithium deep inside, so it reveals mixing and age.
notes.kI: Potassium's resonance line, from the lilac potassium flame Bunsen and Kirchhoff studied in 1860.

dock.markFirst: Mark an element to measure one of its lines
dock.answerHint: Gold lines on the spectrum are each element's lab lines. Keep the elements whose lines land on the spectrum's lines. A star holds every element; you are finding the ones this spectrum shows.
dock.compareHint: Point at an element to preview its lab lines on the spectrum; click to keep them.
dock.mirror: Gold curve: the line mirrored about your marker. A line is symmetric about its centre, so you are on it when the two curves match.

continuum.title: Continuous spectrum
continuum.body: a hot, dense body glows at every wavelength.

absorption.title: Dark lines
absorption.body: the light behind is hotter than the gas, which takes out its own wavelengths.

emission.title: Bright lines
emission.body: with nothing behind it, the gas glows only at its own wavelengths.

reversed.title: Bright lines on a continuum
reversed.body: the gas is hotter than the light behind it.

vanish.title: No lines
vanish.body: gas and light share one temperature: what the gas takes, it gives back.

mysteries.cell: Gas at {temperature} K in front of a {lamp} K lamp
mysteries.giant: A K giant like {star}, at {temperature} K

panel.elementsNote: Mark an element to see its laboratory wavelengths under the spectrum. Pick a line to read it.
panel.resolutionNote: Resolving power R = λ / Δλ: at low R, neighbouring lines blend.
panel.benchNote: The bench gas has a stellar photosphere's electron pressure, so it ionizes as a star's gas would at the same temperature.

rainbow.title: A rainbow with gaps
rainbow.body: Spread sunlight far more finely than raindrops do and the rainbow shows dark gaps. Every element blocks its own set of colours, so the gaps work like a barcode: they tell us what the Sun is made of, without going there.

continuum.title: Light from heat
continuum.body: A hot, dense body glows at every wavelength, brightest where Wien's law puts the peak. This lamp is at the Sun's temperature.

absorption.title: A gas takes its own colours
absorption.body: Sodium vapour in front of the lamp absorbs at 589.0 and 589.6 nm: photons whose energy exactly lifts its outer electron from 3s to 3p.

emission.title: The same lines, glowing
emission.body: Turn the lamp off and the hot gas shines at exactly those wavelengths. Kirchhoff, 1859: a gas absorbs the light it can emit.

hydrogen.title: Hydrogen's ladder
hydrogen.body: Hot hydrogen absorbs the Balmer series, jumps up from n = 2, at wavelengths Rydberg's formula predicts. A cool flame has none: n = 2 is all but empty.

fraunhofer.title: Fraunhofer's dark lines
fraunhofer.body: In 1814 Fraunhofer mapped hundreds of dark lines in sunlight and lettered the strongest. The Sun is a hot photosphere seen through its cooler atmosphere: Kirchhoff's bench, in the sky.

fingerprint.title: Fingerprints
fingerprint.body: When many marked lab lines fall on dark lines at once, the element is there: one match could be chance, a pattern is not.

air.title: Lines from our own air
air.body: At 300 km/s the Sun's lines shift by about λv/c, but the A and B bands stay put: they come from oxygen in Earth's air, which isn't moving.

sequence.title: Temperature, not composition
sequence.body: Modelled with the Sun's composition, Vega still has far stronger hydrogen lines. Near 10,000 K the share of hydrogen in n = 2 peaks; hotter, it ionizes. Payne showed this with Saha's equation in 1925.

cool.title: Cool stars, metal lines
cool.body: At {arcturusK} K more metal atoms stay neutral and many sit in low levels: lines of neutral metals crowd the spectrum while hydrogen's fade.

mystery.title: Your turn
mystery.body: A spectrum with its source hidden. Mark the elements whose lab lines match, slide the gold marker onto the middle of one of their lines to read the velocity, then check.

technicalDetails.title: Inside Stellar Spectra
technicalDetails.summary: Every spectrum here is computed, not drawn: NIST atomic data, Saha–Boltzmann populations and radiative transfer, through a uniform slab on the bench and through ATLAS9 model photospheres for the stars.

features.bench: Kirchhoff's bench: a lamp, a gas and a spectrograph, with dark, bright and vanishing lines from one equation.
features.stars: The Sun and six bright stars from {hottestType} to {coolestType}, and any main-sequence star from {sequenceFromK} to {sequenceToK} K (no M dwarfs).
features.lines: {lines} lines of eight elements from NIST, each with its levels, strength, curve of growth and trend down the spectral sequence.
features.mystery: Mystery cases dealt at random: flames, gas in front of a lamp, stars from B to K, each with its own temperature and velocity.

light.title: Light and photons
light.body: Sources are black bodies (Planck's law). The colours of stars, lamps and flames come from integrating their spectra against the CIE 1931 observer and converting to sRGB. A photon of wavelength λ carries hc/λ: the energy step it can bridge.

atoms.title: Atoms in a hot gas
atoms.body: In local thermodynamic equilibrium, Saha's equation shares an element among its ionization stages and Boltzmann's among the levels of each, with partition functions summed over NIST's levels. The lines are those NIST lists between 380 and 770 nm (air) that are strong enough to show at their species' typical temperature; oscillator strengths come from NIST's transition probabilities, with fine-structure components kept apart (only those NIST lists within 0.002 nm are summed, and hydrogen's lines are its multiplet totals). Wavelengths are quoted in air; photon energies and the physics use vacuum wavelengths.

bench.title: The bench
bench.body: A uniform slab: I = I₀e^(−τ) + B(T)(1 − e^(−τ)). Its gas has an electron pressure of 10 Pa and a gas pressure of 10 kPa, teaching choices set by hand rather than solved from charge balance, so the bench is an idealised slab; the column, the gas temperature and the lamp are yours.

stars.title: Stars
stars.body: Each star is the ATLAS9 model (Castelli & Kurucz 2003) nearest its measured temperature and gravity, with the Sun's composition (Asplund et al. 2009) for its lines; the models themselves were computed with Grevesse & Sauval's (1998), so the pairing is a close hybrid rather than one self-consistent atmosphere. Light is integrated up through 23 layers from τ_Ross = 10⁻⁴ to 10^1.5, each in LTE at its own temperature and pressures. At every wavelength, each layer's continuum opacity comes from H⁻ (John 1988), neutral hydrogen, electron scattering and Rayleigh scattering; the flux is taken in the Eddington–Barbier approximation, F ≈ πI(μ = 2/3). Against the observed Sun, line strengths agree within a factor of 1.7.

shapes.title: Line shapes
shapes.body: Voigt profiles (Humlíček 1982) from thermal and turbulent Doppler broadening, radiation damping, collisions with hydrogen atoms (Barklem, Piskunov & O'Mara 2000 where they list the line, otherwise Unsöld's approximation × 1.15, their median ratio) and, for hydrogen, the linear Stark effect (Gigosos, González & Cardeñoso 2003: their simulated widths for Hα and Hβ, the higher lines scaled from Hβ), with Holtsmark's Δλ^(−5/2) wings. Each layer broadens a line by its own temperature and pressures; hydrogen's shape is taken at τ_Ross = 0.3.

motion.title: Motion and the instrument
motion.body: Radial velocities shift lines by the relativistic Doppler factor. The spectrograph blurs with a Gaussian of full width λ/R, and each pixel averages over its width. Wavelengths are in standard air (Morton 2000).

earth.title: Earth's air
earth.body: The O₂ A and B bands: a rigid-rotor model of their P and R branches from the odd rotational levels of ¹⁶O₂ at 255 K, with measured band origins, rotational constants and strengths, for one airmass.

limits.title: What is left out
limits.body: No molecules besides O₂ (no TiO, so the lab stops at {sequenceFromK} K, short of the M dwarfs), no chromospheres or departures from LTE, no metal bound-free continua (they matter below about 400 nm in cool stars), no hydrogen self-broadening, collisions with helium, rotation or macroturbulence; scattering counts as absorption. In the Sun, strong lines come out up to 1.7 times too strong (Fe I 438 nm); cool stars' Balmer lines are somewhat weak. The scene's photons are schematic.

hr.title: HR diagram
hr.label: Hertzsprung–Russell diagram: {name} among the lab's stars, by temperature and light
hr.labelAll: Hertzsprung–Russell diagram of the lab's stars, by temperature and light
hr.lesson: Dashed lines join stars of equal size: up and to the right means bigger.
